BREAKING: Global fund managers cut their technology exposure by -25 percentage points in early November, to a net 12%, their biggest monthly decline since June 2006.

This marks even a larger monthly decline than during the 2022 bear market or the 2008 Financial Crisis.

As a result, technology is no longer the most overweight sector among fund managers.

The largest overweight positions are currently in Pharmaceuticals, at 34%, and Industrials, at 19%.

A record 38% of surveyed institutional investors believe companies are overinvesting, up from ~20% in January.

At the same time, 52% expect Big Tech companies to announce CapEx reductions over the next 6 months, up from 30% in October.

In Pit Bull: Lessons from Wall Street's Champion Trader Martin Schwartz's autobiography: 

Going for the Gold I

In August 1982, Schwartz hears that Mexico may default on its debt and that US banks could face a run. He panics and sends his wife Audrey to retrieve his gold Krugerrands and Maple Leafs from the bank before it closes.

She brings home a briefcase full of gold worth over $100,000.

Going for the Gold II

During another financial scare, he again rushes to retrieve his gold from a bank safe-deposit box. He describes carrying approximately 40 pounds of gold coins, worth at least $250,000.

He writes:

“Twice now, I'd gone for the gold.”

BREAKING: US margin debt fell -$32 billion in October amid the market's selloff, to $1.45 trillion, but remains at its # level on record.

This follows a combined +$63 billion increase in September and August, and a -$85 billion drop in July.

Year-to-date, margin debt has surged +$223 billion, or +18%.

Since the 2022 bear market low, this metric is up +$842 billion, or +139%.

As a % of M2 money supply, margin debt now stands at 6.2%, its # reading since the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble of 6.4%.

Despite recent volatility, this market remains highly levered.
